description: We are StarKeepers, four young Brazilians who once looked up at the night sky and wondered what we left behind out there. Rovers, landers and probes spent years teaching us about other worlds before going quiet, and we won't let their legacy fade with them. Passionate about making space science exciting and accessible to children, we turn NASA's history into an adventure kids can play, explore and remember.
summary: Forgotten Explorers is a web-based storytelling game that introduces children to the NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars. Players become a young "space journalist" who travels to meet retired robotic explorers. Each explorer speaks in its own voice, and players frame and take photos that build a final album of 14 real NASA machines. Every album entry has facts drawn from NASA's open mission data. The game answers the challenge by turning dense historical and scientific records into play. Kids learn how these missions worked, for example why a rocket waits in orbit just like Apollo 11's Command Module, instead of reading a list of facts. It runs in any browser, on phones, tablets and computers, in English and Portuguese, with no installation needed. These machines made discoveries that shaped how we understand other worlds, yet children rarely hear about them. Forgotten Explorers helps them understand the importance of those quiet pioneers in an accessible and made for children way, because we believe science is for everyone.
details:
Forgotten Explorers is a browser game in which children play a young "space journalist" sent to find NASA machines left behind in space and to bring their stories back to life. After launching from Earth, the player chooses the Moon or Mars, and between missions the rocket docks at the International Space Station.

  • On the Moon, the Lunar Roving Vehicle asks for help. In a platform mini-game, players jump across craters and dodge rolling rocks to find a lost battery. Then they ride the rover and meet the Eagle, the Apollo 11 descent stage.
  • On Mars, Sojourner asks whether Mars once had liquid water. Players then tap passing dust storms, and finally a giant one, to rescue Spirit and Opportunity.

Each machine tells its own story in the first person. Players frame and take their own photos by dragging and zooming the camera. As in Apollo 11, the rocket waits in orbit, and a short "Learn more" panel explains how the Command Module did the same. The game ends with a photo album of 14 real NASA explorers, each with a short text based on NASA mission pages and a link to the source.


Benefits and intended impact
The game turns dense technical and historical records into short, playful moments. Kids learn about the missions by helping the machines and hearing them speak, not by reading lists of facts. We want young players to feel a personal connection to these "metal heroes", understand the science they made possible, and become curious about space exploration.


Tools and technologies

  • Code: a single HTML file written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no external libraries.
  • Graphics and sound: all drawn in code on HTML Canvas, with sound effects and music generated with the Web Audio API.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped develop the code, the illustrations and the English/Portuguese texts, based on our script and on NASA sources. The demo video's voice-over is AI-generated, created with Claude, because our team members are under 18 and the rules did not allow us to use our own voices.

Creativity
The forgotten machines are characters with their own personalities and voices. Each mini-game is linked to a real event: Spirit got stuck in soft sand, and Opportunity went silent during a planet-wide dust storm. The player's photos become the final album, so every player's album is unique.


Factors we considered

  • Age group: short dialogues, simple controls and encouraging feedback, with no "game over".
  • Accessibility: the game runs on phones, tablets and computers with no installation. It has touch and keyboard controls, an English/Portuguese switch and a sound toggle.
  • Accuracy: the facts come from NASA sources, which are cited in the album. The story simplifies some details for children; for example, Apollo 11 did not carry a rover, which was first used on Apollo 15. The album entries give the real mission details.
  • Responsible use: the drawings are original and no NASA logos are used.
